timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

1	# Facts for #230: a web control surface on the remote port
2	
3	Worktree at 7fe8949. No spike was run. The one question that the plan
4	turns on and that no source settles (does iOS Safari open `wss://` to a
5	clicked-through self-signed host?) needs an iPhone, so it goes to the
6	owner. Every other question was settled by the tree or a primary source.
7	
8	## Settled
9	
10	### Tree
11	
12	- The certificate can be reissued over the same key without rotating pairings. `rcgen::KeyPair::from_pem` already reads the Keychain PEM (`src/adapters/remote.rs:139,146`). `CertificateParams` exposes `subject_alt_names`, `not_after` and `extended_key_usages` (`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:58,60,64`). The pin is `sha256(subject_public_key_info)` of the key (`src/adapters/remote.rs:117`), so a new certificate over the same key keeps `spki_sha256`. Today only `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95`) makes certificates, and it always generates a new key (:101), so a reissue path is new code.
13	- The certificate today has no SAN, and its validity runs to 4096-01-01. `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())` is at `src/adapters/remote.rs:102`, and rcgen's default is `not_after = date_time_ymd(4096,1,1)` with `subject_alt_names: Vec::new()` (`rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:85,92`). rcgen turns a string that parses as an IP into `SanType::IpAddress` (`certificate.rs:117`).
14	- The JSON invite is parsed only by the CLI (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:109`), the headset's paste field (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:883`), `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE` (`BrowserView.swift:106`, `client/README.md:180-190`) and the Swift test literal (`client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:161`). Other Swift tests build the `PairingInvite` struct directly, not JSON (for example `client/Tests/SwitchboardClientCoreTests/NewSessionTests.swift:50`), so a URL parser leaves them alone.
15	- Nothing in the remote path logs `request.query`. The only reader is the accessor at `src/adapters/remote.rs:378`, the adapter's one log line is `log::debug!("remote connection: {e}")` (:714), and the `remote:` log lines in `src/app.rs` (1663, 1678, 1716, 2712) name a kind, an id or a code, never a target.
16	- `devices.json` is not under the `model.rs` `SCHEMA_VERSION` rule. `PairedDevice` lives in `src/ports/remote.rs:96`, not `src/core/model.rs` (whose `SCHEMA_VERSION = 16` is at :12). Only `identity.json` has its own version, `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (`src/ports/remote.rs:17`). An additive `#[serde(default)]` field follows `last_seen`.
17	- The card's one-line excerpt for an agent is derived in the UI, not stored. `agent_excerpt` (`src/ui/cards.rs:558-574`) gives the first non-empty line of the last turn's `final_text`, else the last activity line, else `You: <prompt>`, capped at 160 characters. For other kinds it is the pane caption or the host title (`src/ui/cards.rs:177-184`). So no record field holds it, and a wire field would have to compute it on the host from the parsed conversation.
18	- The bearer token is base64url without padding (`src/adapters/remote.rs:340` `URL_SAFE_NO_PAD`). Its alphabet `A-Z a-z 0-9 - _` is entirely RFC 7230 `tchar`, so it is a legal `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` token as it stands.
19	- `respond_upgrade` writes the 101 by hand with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-522`). Echoing one is a change to that format string; tungstenite is not involved in the handshake.
20	- A UI test of the dialog exists: `remote_devices_dialog_opens_pairing_and_revokes_a_device` (`tests/ui.rs:7424`). The script line `pairing <code>|close` exists (`src/script.rs:729-730`).
21	- The embedded page's referenced paths can be a fixed list in the test, because the page has no build step. The precedent for `include_str!`/`include_bytes!` is at `src/main.rs:167` and `src/ui/theme.rs:203-211`. Nothing in the tree parses HTML, so parsing `src=`/`href=` would be new code. This is a plan choice, not a fact gap.
22	
23	### Protocols and standards
24	
25	- A browser's WebSocket handshake carries cookies. It is made with credentials mode `include` (https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/, "establish a WebSocket connection"). The page opens it to its own origin, so the request is same-origin and therefore same-site, and a `SameSite=Strict` cookie is not withheld by SameSite (https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html).
26	- A browser fails the handshake if it offered subprotocols and the 101 does not select one. WHATWG step: if protocols is non-empty and the response `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` is null or empty, "fail the WebSocket connection" (https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/). RFC 6455 §4.2.2 says the selected value must be one the client offered (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.2.2). So the subprotocol route needs the host to echo a value from the offer.
27	- Under the subprotocol route, `new WebSocket(url, [token])` throws `SyntaxError` for a value that is not an RFC 6455 token: printable ASCII U+0021 to U+007E, no separators (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.1, https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/). The token passes (see the tree line above).
28	- Cookies are not isolated by port. A cookie set by `https://<ip>:<port>` is sent to every port on that host (https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html, §1 and §4.1.3.2). With no `Domain` the cookie is host-only (§4.1.2.3, §5.7 step 10). So any other HTTPS service on the Mac's address receives the cookie, and the plan should say so.
29	- A `Secure` cookie is stored and sent only over a channel the browser calls secure (rfc6265bis §4.1.2.5, §5.7 step 13). An `https:` origin is "potentially trustworthy", and the algorithm has no certificate-validity condition (https://www.w3.org/TR/secure-contexts/, §3.1 step 3). Whether a given browser downgrades a page reached through a certificate override is not stated there (see Unresolved).
30	- `connect-src 'self'` covers a same-origin `wss://`. CSP3 §6.7.2.8 step 4 matches when the host matches, the ports are the same, and the URL scheme is `https` or `wss` (https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/). No `wss://host:port` needs naming.
31	- `frame-ancestors` is ignored in a `<meta>` CSP, so it must be a response header (https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/ §3.3).
32	- Safari's tracking prevention deletes all script-writeable storage (localStorage, IndexedDB, `document.cookie` cookies) after 7 days without user interaction with the site. It does not cap first-party `Set-Cookie` cookies. A home-screen web app's domain is exempt (https://webkit.org/tracking-prevention/, "7-Day Cap on All Script-Writeable Storage" and "CNAME and Third-Party IP Address Cloaking Defense"). So a token in `localStorage` is lost after a week unused on iOS Safari; an `HttpOnly` `Set-Cookie` token is not.
33	- Apple's TLS server certificate rules require a SAN carrying the server's name ("all TLS server certificates"). Certificates issued after 2019-07-01 also need validity of 825 days or less and an EKU with `id-kp-serverAuth` (https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769). The current certificate meets none of the three. The page does not say whether the rules apply to a certificate the user clicked through or installed.
34	- A manually installed root is trusted on iOS through Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings, "Enable full trust for root certificates" (https://support.apple.com/en-us/102390). That implies the downloaded certificate must be a CA (basicConstraints CA:TRUE). The article does not state that a leaf cannot be listed.
35	
36	## Unresolved
37	
38	- **Does iOS Safari open `wss://` to a host whose self-signed certificate the user clicked through?** The acceptance criterion depends on this. Evidence conflicts and none of it is from Apple:
39	  - WebKit bug 41419 (open, last modified 2026-01-12): wss to a self-signed host failed on desktop Safari until the certificate was set to always trust (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419).
40	  - Cockpit's documentation: Safari's default WebSocket framework on iOS, iPadOS and ARM Macs refuses wss to self-signed hosts "even when they are manually marked as trusted". This is a project's documentation, so a lead (https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari).
41	  - An Apple forum report that iOS 26 beta 3 failed wss after the page's certificate was accepted, with "The certificate for this server is invalid", and the poster's note that beta 5 resolved it. No Apple reply (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842).
42	
43	  It is not settled because it needs an iPhone and a person's tap through the warning; no source states current behaviour. It goes to the owner.
44	- Whether iOS Safari offers a click-through at all for a certificate with no SAN, or with validity past 825 days. Apple's page states the requirements but not whether the override applies (https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769). Needs a device.
45	- Whether a browser treats a page reached through a certificate override as a secure context. The spec says yes by scheme (https://www.w3.org/TR/secure-contexts/ §3.1), but no browser vendor source was found. Needs a device. It matters for `Secure` cookies and `crypto.randomUUID`.
46	- Whether a QR-opened URL reaches Safari history, the camera's history or iCloud Tabs before `history.replaceState` runs. No source found; Apple does not document it.
47	- Whether a backgrounded or locked iOS Safari tab keeps its WebSocket open. No primary source was found; forum reports exist only for the 2021 "NSURLSession WebSocket" experiment. Plan for a reconnect and resync on `visibilitychange` regardless.
48	- How many parallel connections iOS Safari opens to one origin on page load, and whether it reuses a keep-alive connection within the 30 s idle window. This needs a device and the running host; no source was searched beyond that.
49	- Whether iOS Safari resolves `<name>.local` reliably, and accepts a click-through for a certificate naming it. Not searched to a primary source; needs a device.
50	
51	## For the owner
52	
53	- **Does iOS Safari open the events `wss://` after you accept the certificate warning?** Test on the target iPhone, on the iOS version in use, with a throwaway host.
54	  - Yes: the click-through can be the trust step (decision 1).
55	  - No: either the host offers a CA certificate to install and trust first (reissue with SAN, serverAuth EKU, ≤825 days, CA:TRUE, see Settled), or the page polls REST on a timer in place of the socket.
56	- **Decision 1: click-through or a downloaded certificate?**
57	  - Click-through: reissue the leaf with a SAN for the address and a serverAuth EKU anyway, so the override is offered. Say in the dialog that the browser trusts what you clicked.
58	  - Download: serve a CA certificate before pairing (one more pre-pair path under §5), plus the Certificate Trust Settings steps in the dialog.
59	- **Should the certificate name the IP, and be reissued when the address changes?**
60	  - Yes: reissue on bind over the same key; pins survive.
61	  - No: every address change means a new warning and a new origin, so the browser pairs again.
62	- **Decision 2: cookie or subprotocol?**
63	  - Cookie: `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict`, no `Domain`. It survives ITP and is sent on the socket. Add `Origin` and `Host` checks on POST and on the upgrade, because the cookie is ambient and shared across ports on that IP.
64	  - Subprotocol: echo the offered value in the 101. The token sits in `localStorage`, which ITP deletes after 7 days unused, so the browser re-pairs.
65	- **Should a cookie-authenticated browser reach every endpoint, or only the page's subset?**
66	  - Every endpoint: no new allowlist.
67	  - Subset: a second allowlist keyed on how the request authenticated.
68	- **Decision 3: keep the JSON invite?**
69	  - Drop it: change the four JSON parsers listed under Settled to read the URL; the URL carries one address.
70	  - Keep it: those parsers accept both forms.
71	- **Which address goes in the URL when the Mac has several, and should an IPv6 address be bracketed?**
72	  - One address: the routed one from `local_address()`, written `[addr]:port` for IPv6.
73	  - A `.local` name: depends on the unresolved `.local` question.
74	- **Decision 4: static paths and headers.** The exact set; whether unknown non-API paths 404; `Cache-Control: no-store` or versioned paths; `frame-ancestors` and the rest as headers (`<meta>` cannot carry `frame-ancestors`). Serve on the connection thread or through the frame? Which pool and rate window does a page load use?
75	  - Connection thread: the frame never sees static loads.
76	  - Frame: as today.
77	- **What does the page show with neither a code nor a token?**
78	  - `/info` data: the host name and `pairing_open`, with "scan the QR".
79	  - Static text only.
80	- **Decision 6: device name from `User-Agent` on the host, or `navigator.userAgent` on the page? Add a `kind` field to `PairedDevice`?**
81	  - Add `kind`: an additive `#[serde(default)]` field, no version needed (see Settled).
82	  - No `kind`: the name alone tells devices apart.
83	- **The card excerpt on the page.**
84	  - A `SessionView` field: compute `agent_excerpt`'s rule on the host, update the fixtures and the fingerprint.
85	  - A `last-response` read per session: N reads per list.
86	  - Drop it.
87	- **The device's scope after a reload.**
88	  - A tiny who-am-I endpoint: a new read model.
89	  - Page storage: subject to ITP's 7-day deletion.
90	  - A `403 scope`: the reply box shows until a send fails.
91	- **Telling revoked from identity-changed.**
92	  - Distinct 401 codes: a wire change.
93	  - The page keeps the server id and key per origin: storage subject to ITP.
94	- **What the session view shows for a stopped session that is not Claude Code (screen is refused).**
95	  - Last run output.
96	  - A note saying there is nothing to show.
97	- **In this cut: plain `send` or drafts, Resume and Trust on the page, full §4.4 subscribe-then-snapshot, `watch`/`unwatch`, the 30 s refetch.**
98	  - Yes: the page mirrors the headset.
99	  - No: the page reads only `changed`.
100	- **Advertise a `web` capability in `/info` or TXT?**

# Facts for #230: a web control surface on the remote port

Worktree at 7fe8949. No spike was run. The one question that the plan
turns on and that no source settles (does iOS Safari open `wss://` to a
clicked-through self-signed host?) needs an iPhone, so it goes to the
owner. Every other question was settled by the tree or a primary source.

## Settled

### Tree

- The certificate can be reissued over the same key without rotating pairings. `rcgen::KeyPair::from_pem` already reads the Keychain PEM (`src/adapters/remote.rs:139,146`). `CertificateParams` exposes `subject_alt_names`, `not_after` and `extended_key_usages` (`~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:58,60,64`). The pin is `sha256(subject_public_key_info)` of the key (`src/adapters/remote.rs:117`), so a new certificate over the same key keeps `spki_sha256`. Today only `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95`) makes certificates, and it always generates a new key (:101), so a reissue path is new code.
- The certificate today has no SAN, and its validity runs to 4096-01-01. `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())` is at `src/adapters/remote.rs:102`, and rcgen's default is `not_after = date_time_ymd(4096,1,1)` with `subject_alt_names: Vec::new()` (`rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:85,92`). rcgen turns a string that parses as an IP into `SanType::IpAddress` (`certificate.rs:117`).
- The JSON invite is parsed only by the CLI (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:109`), the headset's paste field (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:883`), `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE` (`BrowserView.swift:106`, `client/README.md:180-190`) and the Swift test literal (`client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:161`). Other Swift tests build the `PairingInvite` struct directly, not JSON (for example `client/Tests/SwitchboardClientCoreTests/NewSessionTests.swift:50`), so a URL parser leaves them alone.
- Nothing in the remote path logs `request.query`. The only reader is the accessor at `src/adapters/remote.rs:378`, the adapter's one log line is `log::debug!("remote connection: {e}")` (:714), and the `remote:` log lines in `src/app.rs` (1663, 1678, 1716, 2712) name a kind, an id or a code, never a target.
- `devices.json` is not under the `model.rs` `SCHEMA_VERSION` rule. `PairedDevice` lives in `src/ports/remote.rs:96`, not `src/core/model.rs` (whose `SCHEMA_VERSION = 16` is at :12). Only `identity.json` has its own version, `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (`src/ports/remote.rs:17`). An additive `#[serde(default)]` field follows `last_seen`.
- The card's one-line excerpt for an agent is derived in the UI, not stored. `agent_excerpt` (`src/ui/cards.rs:558-574`) gives the first non-empty line of the last turn's `final_text`, else the last activity line, else `You: <prompt>`, capped at 160 characters. For other kinds it is the pane caption or the host title (`src/ui/cards.rs:177-184`). So no record field holds it, and a wire field would have to compute it on the host from the parsed conversation.
- The bearer token is base64url without padding (`src/adapters/remote.rs:340` `URL_SAFE_NO_PAD`). Its alphabet `A-Z a-z 0-9 - _` is entirely RFC 7230 `tchar`, so it is a legal `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` token as it stands.
- `respond_upgrade` writes the 101 by hand with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-522`). Echoing one is a change to that format string; tungstenite is not involved in the handshake.
- A UI test of the dialog exists: `remote_devices_dialog_opens_pairing_and_revokes_a_device` (`tests/ui.rs:7424`). The script line `pairing <code>|close` exists (`src/script.rs:729-730`).
- The embedded page's referenced paths can be a fixed list in the test, because the page has no build step. The precedent for `include_str!`/`include_bytes!` is at `src/main.rs:167` and `src/ui/theme.rs:203-211`. Nothing in the tree parses HTML, so parsing `src=`/`href=` would be new code. This is a plan choice, not a fact gap.

### Protocols and standards

- A browser's WebSocket handshake carries cookies. It is made with credentials mode `include` (https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/, "establish a WebSocket connection"). The page opens it to its own origin, so the request is same-origin and therefore same-site, and a `SameSite=Strict` cookie is not withheld by SameSite (https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html).
- A browser fails the handshake if it offered subprotocols and the 101 does not select one. WHATWG step: if protocols is non-empty and the response `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` is null or empty, "fail the WebSocket connection" (https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/). RFC 6455 §4.2.2 says the selected value must be one the client offered (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.2.2). So the subprotocol route needs the host to echo a value from the offer.
- Under the subprotocol route, `new WebSocket(url, [token])` throws `SyntaxError` for a value that is not an RFC 6455 token: printable ASCII U+0021 to U+007E, no separators (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-4.1, https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/). The token passes (see the tree line above).
- Cookies are not isolated by port. A cookie set by `https://<ip>:<port>` is sent to every port on that host (https://httpwg.org/http-extensions/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis.html, §1 and §4.1.3.2). With no `Domain` the cookie is host-only (§4.1.2.3, §5.7 step 10). So any other HTTPS service on the Mac's address receives the cookie, and the plan should say so.
- A `Secure` cookie is stored and sent only over a channel the browser calls secure (rfc6265bis §4.1.2.5, §5.7 step 13). An `https:` origin is "potentially trustworthy", and the algorithm has no certificate-validity condition (https://www.w3.org/TR/secure-contexts/, §3.1 step 3). Whether a given browser downgrades a page reached through a certificate override is not stated there (see Unresolved).
- `connect-src 'self'` covers a same-origin `wss://`. CSP3 §6.7.2.8 step 4 matches when the host matches, the ports are the same, and the URL scheme is `https` or `wss` (https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/). No `wss://host:port` needs naming.
- `frame-ancestors` is ignored in a `<meta>` CSP, so it must be a response header (https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/ §3.3).
- Safari's tracking prevention deletes all script-writeable storage (localStorage, IndexedDB, `document.cookie` cookies) after 7 days without user interaction with the site. It does not cap first-party `Set-Cookie` cookies. A home-screen web app's domain is exempt (https://webkit.org/tracking-prevention/, "7-Day Cap on All Script-Writeable Storage" and "CNAME and Third-Party IP Address Cloaking Defense"). So a token in `localStorage` is lost after a week unused on iOS Safari; an `HttpOnly` `Set-Cookie` token is not.
- Apple's TLS server certificate rules require a SAN carrying the server's name ("all TLS server certificates"). Certificates issued after 2019-07-01 also need validity of 825 days or less and an EKU with `id-kp-serverAuth` (https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769). The current certificate meets none of the three. The page does not say whether the rules apply to a certificate the user clicked through or installed.
- A manually installed root is trusted on iOS through Settings > General > About > Certificate Trust Settings, "Enable full trust for root certificates" (https://support.apple.com/en-us/102390). That implies the downloaded certificate must be a CA (basicConstraints CA:TRUE). The article does not state that a leaf cannot be listed.

## Unresolved

- **Does iOS Safari open `wss://` to a host whose self-signed certificate the user clicked through?** The acceptance criterion depends on this. Evidence conflicts and none of it is from Apple:
  - WebKit bug 41419 (open, last modified 2026-01-12): wss to a self-signed host failed on desktop Safari until the certificate was set to always trust (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419).
  - Cockpit's documentation: Safari's default WebSocket framework on iOS, iPadOS and ARM Macs refuses wss to self-signed hosts "even when they are manually marked as trusted". This is a project's documentation, so a lead (https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari).
  - An Apple forum report that iOS 26 beta 3 failed wss after the page's certificate was accepted, with "The certificate for this server is invalid", and the poster's note that beta 5 resolved it. No Apple reply (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842).

  It is not settled because it needs an iPhone and a person's tap through the warning; no source states current behaviour. It goes to the owner.
- Whether iOS Safari offers a click-through at all for a certificate with no SAN, or with validity past 825 days. Apple's page states the requirements but not whether the override applies (https://support.apple.com/en-us/103769). Needs a device.
- Whether a browser treats a page reached through a certificate override as a secure context. The spec says yes by scheme (https://www.w3.org/TR/secure-contexts/ §3.1), but no browser vendor source was found. Needs a device. It matters for `Secure` cookies and `crypto.randomUUID`.
- Whether a QR-opened URL reaches Safari history, the camera's history or iCloud Tabs before `history.replaceState` runs. No source found; Apple does not document it.
- Whether a backgrounded or locked iOS Safari tab keeps its WebSocket open. No primary source was found; forum reports exist only for the 2021 "NSURLSession WebSocket" experiment. Plan for a reconnect and resync on `visibilitychange` regardless.
- How many parallel connections iOS Safari opens to one origin on page load, and whether it reuses a keep-alive connection within the 30 s idle window. This needs a device and the running host; no source was searched beyond that.
- Whether iOS Safari resolves `<name>.local` reliably, and accepts a click-through for a certificate naming it. Not searched to a primary source; needs a device.

## For the owner

- **Does iOS Safari open the events `wss://` after you accept the certificate warning?** Test on the target iPhone, on the iOS version in use, with a throwaway host.
  - Yes: the click-through can be the trust step (decision 1).
  - No: either the host offers a CA certificate to install and trust first (reissue with SAN, serverAuth EKU, ≤825 days, CA:TRUE, see Settled), or the page polls REST on a timer in place of the socket.
- **Decision 1: click-through or a downloaded certificate?**
  - Click-through: reissue the leaf with a SAN for the address and a serverAuth EKU anyway, so the override is offered. Say in the dialog that the browser trusts what you clicked.
  - Download: serve a CA certificate before pairing (one more pre-pair path under §5), plus the Certificate Trust Settings steps in the dialog.
- **Should the certificate name the IP, and be reissued when the address changes?**
  - Yes: reissue on bind over the same key; pins survive.
  - No: every address change means a new warning and a new origin, so the browser pairs again.
- **Decision 2: cookie or subprotocol?**
  - Cookie: `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict`, no `Domain`. It survives ITP and is sent on the socket. Add `Origin` and `Host` checks on POST and on the upgrade, because the cookie is ambient and shared across ports on that IP.
  - Subprotocol: echo the offered value in the 101. The token sits in `localStorage`, which ITP deletes after 7 days unused, so the browser re-pairs.
- **Should a cookie-authenticated browser reach every endpoint, or only the page's subset?**
  - Every endpoint: no new allowlist.
  - Subset: a second allowlist keyed on how the request authenticated.
- **Decision 3: keep the JSON invite?**
  - Drop it: change the four JSON parsers listed under Settled to read the URL; the URL carries one address.
  - Keep it: those parsers accept both forms.
- **Which address goes in the URL when the Mac has several, and should an IPv6 address be bracketed?**
  - One address: the routed one from `local_address()`, written `[addr]:port` for IPv6.
  - A `.local` name: depends on the unresolved `.local` question.
- **Decision 4: static paths and headers.** The exact set; whether unknown non-API paths 404; `Cache-Control: no-store` or versioned paths; `frame-ancestors` and the rest as headers (`<meta>` cannot carry `frame-ancestors`). Serve on the connection thread or through the frame? Which pool and rate window does a page load use?
  - Connection thread: the frame never sees static loads.
  - Frame: as today.
- **What does the page show with neither a code nor a token?**
  - `/info` data: the host name and `pairing_open`, with "scan the QR".
  - Static text only.
- **Decision 6: device name from `User-Agent` on the host, or `navigator.userAgent` on the page? Add a `kind` field to `PairedDevice`?**
  - Add `kind`: an additive `#[serde(default)]` field, no version needed (see Settled).
  - No `kind`: the name alone tells devices apart.
- **The card excerpt on the page.**
  - A `SessionView` field: compute `agent_excerpt`'s rule on the host, update the fixtures and the fingerprint.
  - A `last-response` read per session: N reads per list.
  - Drop it.
- **The device's scope after a reload.**
  - A tiny who-am-I endpoint: a new read model.
  - Page storage: subject to ITP's 7-day deletion.
  - A `403 scope`: the reply box shows until a send fails.
- **Telling revoked from identity-changed.**
  - Distinct 401 codes: a wire change.
  - The page keeps the server id and key per origin: storage subject to ITP.
- **What the session view shows for a stopped session that is not Claude Code (screen is refused).**
  - Last run output.
  - A note saying there is nothing to show.
- **In this cut: plain `send` or drafts, Resume and Trust on the page, full §4.4 subscribe-then-snapshot, `watch`/`unwatch`, the 30 s refetch.**
  - Yes: the page mirrors the headset.
  - No: the page reads only `changed`.
- **Advertise a `web` capability in `/info` or TXT?**
  - Yes: an additive field.
  - No: nothing changes.
- **Acceptance on a real phone:** scan, click through, see sessions, watch a session move to waiting, reply, revoke. Needs a device on the same network and the signed bundle.

1	# Issue #230 — a web control surface on the remote port: investigation notes
2	
3	Read first: `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/design.md` (core idea, Durable store,
4	Trust boundary, "Remote client (2026-10-12)" status at line 3107 on),
5	`docs/lessons.md`, `docs/remote-client.md` §4.1–§5 and §9–§11. Line
6	numbers are as they are in this worktree (branch
7	`dispatch/230-a-web-control-surface-the-remote-port-se`, at 7fe8949).
8	There is no `web/` directory yet.
9	
10	## Record and rehydration first
11	
12	**What is on disk today.**
13	
14	- `<data dir>/identity.json` (`ports/remote.rs:26` `Identity`,
15	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at :17): server id, display name, the
16	  self-signed certificate (DER, base64), its `spki_sha256`, `listen
17	  {lan, port}`. The private key is a Keychain item `remote-key:<id>`
18	  (:49).
19	- `<data dir>/devices.json` (`ports/remote.rs:96` `PairedDevice`): `id,
20	  name, scope, token_sha256, created, last_seen` per device. It is a
21	  bare JSON array written by `RemoteFiles::save_devices`
22	  (`adapters/remote.rs:83`) through `JsonStore`; it carries **no
23	  `schema_version` of its own** (only `identity.json` does), and
24	  `last_seen` is already a `#[serde(default)]` field, which is the
25	  precedent for additive fields here.
26	- The pairing window is core state only, never saved:
27	  `PairingWindow {until, code, scope, failures}` (`core/action.rs`
28	  around :290, `PAIRING_WINDOW` 5 min and `PAIRING_ATTEMPTS` 3 at
29	  :972–973), set by `OpenPairing` (`core/remote.rs:46`), spent by
30	  `Paired` (:64), counted by `PairingFailed` (:56).
31	
32	**What a browser device adds to the record.** Nothing new is
33	required: a browser is a `PairedDevice` like the headset and the CLI.
34	`/pair` already takes `device_name` from the body (`app.rs:3650`) and
35	`new_device` (`core/remote.rs:166`) takes the window's scope, caps the
36	name at 64 chars, and keeps only the token hash. A "kind" field
37	(browser vs native) or a stored user-agent string would be an
38	additive `#[serde(default)]` field on `PairedDevice`; whether that
39	needs a version on `devices.json` is open (below). The token hash is
40	the same whether the token travels as a bearer header or a cookie, so
41	the record does not depend on decision 2.
42	
43	**Rehydration.** Host side: unchanged. On start `IdentityLoaded`
44	brings back identity and devices; a browser token stays valid across
45	host restarts because only its hash is checked
46	(`AppCore::device_by_token`, `core/remote.rs:146`). Revocation removes
47	the record (`RevokeDevice`, :84) and drops that device's subscribers
48	(`app.rs:486–498`). Key rotation clears `devices.json`, which
49	invalidates a browser's token the same as any other.
50	
51	Device side: there is no record on the device except what the browser
52	keeps for the origin `https://<address>:<port>`. That is the whole of
53	a browser's "rehydration": the token (cookie or storage), and anything
54	the page chooses to keep (server id, scope, last-known key). The
55	origin includes the address, so **a host whose DHCP address changes is
56	a different origin to the browser**: the cookie/storage and the
57	accepted certificate exception do not follow it, and the device has to
58	pair again from a fresh QR. The native clients do not have this
59	problem because they pin the key and re-resolve via Bonjour (§6.1).
60	Page content itself is never durable on the device beyond the
61	browser's cache, which decision 4 wants off.
62	
63	The page's own files are not a record at all: they are compiled into
64	the binary (`include_str!`/`include_bytes!` — precedent at
65	`src/main.rs:167` and `src/ui/theme.rs:203–211`), so a host's version
66	and its page's version can never drift.
67	
68	## Where the code is
69	
70	### Listener: `src/adapters/remote.rs`
71	
72	- `RemoteRequest` (:360–372): `method`, `path` (query stripped),
73	  `query` (pairs, **undecoded**, :497–504), `body`, `bearer`,
74	  `upgrade`. No `Cookie`, no `Origin`, no `Host`, no `User-Agent`, no
75	  `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, no `Accept` is kept; every other header is
76	  parsed into a local `headers` vec and thrown away (:456–480).
77	- `read_request` (:444): bearer read only as `Authorization: Bearer `
78	  (case-sensitive prefix, :487–490); upgrade recognised from `Upgrade:
79	  websocket` + `Sec-WebSocket-Key` (:491–494). Head cap 8 KiB, body
80	  cap 64 KiB (:437–438).
81	- `respond` (:530–553) **hard-codes `Content-Type: application/json`**
82	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, and has no way to add a header
83	  (`Set-Cookie`, `Content-Security-Policy`, `Cache-Control`,
84	  `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`). `RemoteReply`
85	  (:389–393) is `{status, body, authenticated}` with no content type
86	  or headers. Reason phrases for 101 is separate (`respond_upgrade`,
87	  :519–527); 304/302 are not in the reason table.
88	- `respond_upgrade` (:519): writes the 101 with
89	  `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` only; it does **not** echo a
90	  `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, which matters if decision 2 picks the
91	  subprotocol route (a browser fails the handshake if it offered a
92	  protocol and the server does not select one — to be confirmed,
93	  below).
94	- Pools (:564–568): `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`. The
95	  accept loop closes a fifth unauthenticated connection at once
96	  (:699–707). A connection moves to the paired pool only when the
97	  frame answers `authenticated: true` (:834–848).
98	- Rate windows (:582–587, :623–640): `/api/v1/pair` 6/min, `/api/v1/info`
99	  60/min, per listener, sliding (`RateWindow`, :596). Any other path is
100	  never limited (`Limits::limited` returns false, :634).
101	- Deadlines (:570–577): 5 s handshake and first line, 30 s idle between
102	  requests, 10 s write, 60 s for the frame's answer.
103	- `connection` (:770): one request in flight, the 429 and 503 answered
104	  without the frame, then hands to the frame over the 64-deep channel.
105	- `subscriber` (:878): the WebSocket, `tungstenite::from_raw_socket`
106	  after the hand-written 101.
107	- `make_identity` (:95–127): `CertificateParams::new(vec![])` — **no
108	  subjectAltName at all**, CN `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's
109	  default validity (comment says `not_after` year 4096), P-256 key.
110	  `tls_config` (:144): rustls with ring, safe default versions.
111	  `local_address()` (:962): the routed outward IP, v4 or v6.
112	
113	### Frame side: `src/app.rs`
114	
115	- The pump: `app.rs:1586–1597` drains `DRAIN_PER_PASS` requests and
116	  calls `serve_remote`.
117	- `serve_remote` (:3017–3123): `strip_prefix("/api/v1/")` at :3023 —
118	  anything else is `404 not_found "no such endpoint"`; this is where
119	  `GET /` and the page's files would be matched (or before it, in the
120	  adapter). `info` and `pair` before auth (:3027–3031); everything
121	  else through `authenticate` (:3127), which reads only
122	  `request.bearer`. Events at :3036; the allowlist :3044–3116.
123	- `authenticate` (:3127–3153): no bearer → 401 `unauthorized` "pair
124	  this device first"; unknown token → 401 `unauthorized` "the token is
125	  not known; pair again". A **revoked** token and a **rotated** host
126	  both land on the second message; nothing in the reply tells
127	  "revoked" from "never paired here" from "host key changed".
128	- `remote_subscribe` (:2723–2758): accepts the upgrade, queues `hello`.
129	- `remote_info` (:3568–3600): `server_id`, `server_name`, `protocol`,
130	  `capabilities`, `spki_sha256`, `version`, `limits`, `pairing_open`.
131	  Note `spki_sha256` here is a **self-report in the body**, not
132	  something the page can check against the TLS key it is talking to.
133	- `remote_pair` (:3606–3670): requires the window, `spki_sha256 ==
134	  identity.spki_sha256` (:3633), the code (case-insensitive, :3643);
135	  reply `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in the envelope.
136	- `refuse` (:3754–3772) logs `method` and `path` only. Because `path`
137	  excludes the query, a `GET /?code=…&key=…` would not log the code;
138	  but `request.query` keeps it in memory and any future log of the
139	  target would leak it.
140	- Revocation closing sockets: `dispatch_inner` :486–498.
141	- `Subscriber` (:242–249) keys subscribers by device id, so a browser's
142	  socket closes on Revoke like any other — provided the browser's
143	  socket authenticated as that device.

145	### Pairing window: `src/ui/remote.rs`
146	
147	- `pairing` (:141–227): the QR payload is built **in the UI** with
148	  `serde_json::json!({server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses})`
149	  (:160–166) and `remote::local_address()` is called **on every frame
150	  while the window is open** (:157), which is I/O from `ui/`. CLAUDE.md
151	  says logic under `ui/` moves to the core; the URL form is a natural

153	  with a test, and to cache the address.
154	- `addresses` is `"{ip}:{port}"` (:157–159); for an IPv6 address that
155	  string is not a valid URL authority — a URL needs `[ip]:port`.
156	- "Copy invite" (:201–207) copies the same JSON.
157	- The texture cache is keyed by the code (:167–172); a payload that
158	  changes for another reason (address, port) while the code holds is
159	  not redrawn.
160	- Scope radio (:212–218): the hover on Control still says "later the
161	  commands", stale since C3.
162	- Paired devices list (:230–276): name, scope combo, paired, seen,
163	  Revoke. No column says what kind of device it is.
164	- Redaction sentence (:72) is where a "the browser trusted this

167	
168	### Core: `src/core/remote.rs`
169	
170	As above; `new_device` (:166) and the window. No change needed for a

176	  `PairingInvite` is `Decodable` with `server_id`, `spki_sha256`,

178	- Callers of `PairingInvite.parse`: the CLI

185	  `client/README.md:180–190`), and the Swift test
186	  `FixturesTests.swift:157` (a JSON literal, not a Rust-written
187	  fixture). README.md:277 documents `switchboard-remote pair
188	  "$(pbpaste)"`.
189	- A URL carries one address; the JSON carries a list. The CLI's device
190	  name is `"<hostname> (cli)"` (`main.swift:33`).
191	
192	### Tests
193	
194	- `tests/remote.rs` (44 tests): `http(addr, config, method, path,
195	  bearer, body)` at :245 is the host's own pinned client — it builds
196	  the request with a bearer only, no cookie or arbitrary headers, and
197	  returns `(status, body String)` without response headers. A test of
198	  `Content-Type`/CSP/`Set-Cookie` needs it to return headers. `pair`
199	  helper :406. The fixture writer :1579–1700 writes
200	  `client/Fixtures/*.json` (`SWITCHBOARD_WRITE_FIXTURES=1`).
201	- The allowlist test (:682) asserts non-`/api/v1` refusal behaviour
202	  that the page paths will change.
203	- The stalled-strangers test (README layout line for tests/remote.rs)
204	  depends on the 4-slot pool.
205	
206	## What the page needs that the wire does not have
207	
208	These are findings from reading the tree, each checked against the
209	code:
210	
211	1. **The card's one-line excerpt is not on the wire.** The issue asks
212	   for "the one-line excerpt the card shows". §4.3 (spec) says that is
213	   `last_message` from the Stop hook, "a field of the session's
214	   metadata", but `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637–688`) has no
215	   `last_message`; it has `card` (the card's word), `waiting_reason`,
216	   `notes`. So either an additive field on `SessionView` (a wire
217	   change touching the Swift fixtures and `revision.rs`'s fingerprint),
218	   or a fetch of `last-response` per listed session (a content read
219	   each), or the page drops the excerpt.
220	2. **The device's own scope has no read endpoint.** It comes back only
221	   in the `/pair` reply (`app.rs:3660–3665`). The Swift client keeps it
222	   from there (`ServerConnection.swift:232`) and learns a lowered scope
223	   from a `403 scope` refusal. A page reloaded later (and with an
224	   `HttpOnly` cookie, which the script cannot read) cannot show "the
225	   device's scope" or decide to hide the reply box without either
226	   keeping scope in page storage, or a new tiny endpoint (who am I:
227	   device name and scope), which the issue says to avoid unless needed.
228	   Raising scope in the dialog is invisible to the page until it asks.
229	3. **"Revoked" and "identity changed" are not distinguishable from the
230	   replies.** Both are the same 401 `unauthorized`. The native client
231	   learns "identity changed" from the TLS pin failing, which the
232	   browser cannot see; a rotated host serves a new certificate, so the
233	   browser shows a certificate warning again before the page even
234	   loads, and after the click-through the page sees `/info`'s new
235	   `spki_sha256` and the same 401. The page can only say "identity
236	   changed" if it kept the old key/server id per origin (page storage)
237	   and compares.
238	4. **Screen for a stopped session.** `session.screen` refuses a
239	   session that is not running (spec §4.3), and only Claude Code has a
240	   last response; so a stopped shell/command/Codex session has nothing
241	   to show except `runs/{n}/output` for a command or service. The
242	   issue's "the screen for anything else" needs a plan for that case.
243	5. **Grouping by project costs N+1 reads.** Sessions are listed per
244	   project (`projects/{id}/sessions`); `waiting` is global. The page
245	   would read `projects` then each project's sessions, refetching a
246	   project's list on `changed {sessions, project}` — the headset does
247	   the same; fine at this scale but worth naming.
248	6. **Unauthenticated page loads use the 4-slot pool.** A page load
249	   (`/`, CSS, JS, `/info`) is unauthenticated until a request carries
250	   the token; browsers commonly open several parallel connections to
251	   one origin, and a fifth is dropped at accept. Static files also do
252	   not move a connection to the paired pool (`authenticated` is set
253	   only by the frame for a known token). Whether the page's assets
254	   should be served from the connection thread (no frame, like the
255	   429) and whether a cookie-bearing static request should count as
256	   paired are plan decisions.
257	7. **The key check in the URL protects less than it looks.** The page
258	   cannot read the TLS key it is connected to; it can only compare the
259	   URL's `key` with `/info`'s self-reported `spki_sha256`. An impostor
260	   that relays will report the genuine key in `/info` and pass that
261	   check, and the host's `wrong_key` check (`app.rs:3633`) also passes
262	   because the page sends the genuine key from the URL. So for a
263	   browser, §5's "key verified before the code is sent" is replaced by
264	   whatever the certificate trust step gives; the URL key only catches
265	   a QR pointing at the wrong host by mistake, or a stale QR. Decision
266	   1 has to say this plainly.
267	8. **Cookie or subprotocol auth needs adapter changes either way.**
268	   `read_request` must keep the cookie (or `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`)
269	   value next to `bearer`, never in logged fields; `respond` must be
270	   able to send `Set-Cookie` (or `respond_upgrade` must echo the
271	   selected subprotocol). With a cookie, the API becomes reachable by
272	   ambient credentials, so `Origin` (and probably `Host`) checking on
273	   state-changing requests and on the WebSocket upgrade becomes
274	   necessary; today nothing reads `Origin` because no browser could
275	   authenticate.
276	9. **Logic in `ui/remote.rs`.** The invite payload and the address
277	   lookup live in the dialog; the URL form should be a pure, tested
278	   function, with IPv6 bracketing.
279	
280	## Pane last
281	
282	Only after the above: a static page (HTML + one CSS + one JS, no
283	framework) served at the port root, sessions grouped by project with
284	waiting first, a session view (last response or screen), a reply box
285	under control scope, header with host name and scope, explicit
286	"identity changed, pair again" and "revoked" states. On the Mac side
287	the dialog's QR changes to the URL, possibly the device list gains a
288	kind, and a sentence about the browser's trust step. The UI test for
289	the dialog (`tests/ui.rs`) would assert the invite text through "Copy
290	invite" or the core; I did not look for an existing test of the
291	dialog.
292	
293	## What I did not check
294	
295	- I did not run anything: no build, no tests, no browser, no phone.
296	- I did not read the Swift transport/core beyond the pair path and the
297	  scope handling lines named above, nor `client/README.md` beyond the
298	  invite lines.
299	- I did not read `tests/ui.rs` for an existing Remote devices dialog
300	  test, nor `src/script.rs` for the `pairing` script line's shape
301	  beyond the README mention (README.md:318).
302	- I did not read the conversation/last-response handlers
303	  (`app.rs:1947–2125`) in detail, nor `revision.rs`.
304	- I did not check `Cargo.toml` features of `rcgen` (SAN/EKU/validity
305	  options) or `tungstenite`'s subprotocol handling.
306	- Nothing outside the tree was consulted; every browser and platform
307	  claim in the issue is listed below as a question.
308	
309	## Open questions
310	
311	- [owner] Decision 1: is the click-through on the local network the trust step (said in the dialog), or does the host offer its certificate for download to trust on the device first?
312	- [source] Does iOS/iPadOS Safari let a page whose self-signed certificate was clicked through open a `wss://` WebSocket to the same origin, or does the socket fail where `fetch` succeeds?
313	- [source] Does Safari on iOS offer a click-through at all for a certificate with no subjectAltName (the current cert has none), and for a certificate whose validity runs to year 4096 (Apple's TLS server certificate requirements: SAN required, at most 825 days, serverAuth EKU)?
314	- [source] If the certificate is downloaded and trusted on the device instead, what must it carry (SAN with the IP address, validity limit, EKU, basicConstraints for a self-signed root) and how is it installed (profile, then Certificate Trust Settings)?
315	- [tree] Can the certificate be reissued over the same Keychain key with a SAN and a shorter validity without rotating pairings (the pin is the SPKI, so §5 says yes) — and where would reissue run (`make_identity` today only makes new keys)?
316	- [owner] If the certificate names an IP address, what happens when the Mac's address changes: reissue on every bind, or accept the mismatch as part of the click-through?
317	- [source] Does a browser treat a page served over a clicked-through self-signed certificate as a secure context (needed for `crypto.randomUUID`, `Secure` cookies, and some APIs)?
318	- [owner] Decision 2: `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie, or the token as a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value (with the token then held in page storage)?
319	- [source] Does a browser send a `SameSite=Strict` cookie on a same-origin `new WebSocket()` handshake, in Safari and Chrome both?
320	- [source] If the subprotocol route is chosen: what characters may a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` token carry (the bearer is base64url), and does a browser fail the handshake when the server's 101 does not echo a selected protocol?
321	- [source] Does a cookie set by a response on `https://<ip>:<port>` with no `Domain` stay scoped to that host and port, and does Safari's tracking prevention or ITP expire it?
322	- [owner] With a cookie: should the host check `Origin` on every POST and on the WebSocket upgrade, and `Host` against its own addresses (a DNS rebinding guard), and refuse when absent or foreign?
323	- [owner] Should a cookie-authenticated browser be able to read every endpoint the bearer can, or only the subset the page uses (tickets, drafts, dictation, new session are out of this cut)?
324	- [owner] Decision 3: one QR (the URL) read by the browser, the CLI and the headset's paste field, with the JSON dropped — or keep the JSON form as well, and for how long?
325	- [tree] Do any other consumers of the JSON invite exist besides the CLI, the headset paste field, `SWITCHBOARD_INVITE`, and the Swift `FixturesTests` literal?
326	- [owner] The URL carries one address while the JSON carries a list: which address goes in the URL when the Mac has several, and how is an IPv6 address written (`[addr]:port`)?

329	- [owner] Decision 4: the exact static paths (`/`, `/app.js`, `/app.css`, an icon?), and whether `/index.html` or unknown non-API paths 404 or fall back to `/`.
